item.title: UK threatens subsea cable saboteurs with 14 years behind bars
item.description:
Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of keeping Russian submarines away from critical infrastructure.

The government on Thursday set out plans to overhaul legislation dating back to 1885 and introduce tougher penalties for damaging the underwater cables and pipelines that keep Britain's internet and energy supplies running.

According to Whitehall, subsea cables carry around 99 percent of the UK's international data traffic, while underwater pipelines account for 74 percent of its gas supply. Yet much of this infrastructure is protected by laws written when the telegraph was cutting-edge technology.

The Submarine Telegraph Act 1885 originally imposed a £100 maximum fine for damaging a cable through culpable negligence. That might have been a reasonable deterrent back then, but it's unlikely to give today's would-be saboteurs much pause.

Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical subsea energy or telecoms infrastructure could face up to 14 years behind bars. The proposals also set tougher penalties, including unlimited fines, for reckless or negligent damage.

Subsea telecoms operators would face new legal duties to identify and manage security risks, while ministers would gain powers to direct companies and cable repair providers to take action where necessary and proportionate to protect national security.

The government also wants to regulate fiber-optic sensing technology, which uses subsea cables to detect activity at sea but could pose a security risk if sensitive data falls into hostile hands.

Unsurprisingly, Russia features prominently in Whitehall's thinking.

In April, British forces exposed a covert Russian submarine operation near critical undersea infrastructure. The operation reportedly involved an attack submarine acting as a decoy while two specialist vessels surveyed Britain's cable routes.

"The threats we face have changed dramatically, with suspicious Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure, yet some of the laws protecting these vital connections date back more than a century," said telecoms minister Ian Murray.

The plans aren't entirely new. In May, the government announced its intention to toughen penalties and introduce security obligations for cable operators. Thursday's White Paper spells out the proposed penalties and how far ministers could go in directing operators to act.

It also follows warnings from Parliament's Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, which concluded last year that Britain was insufficiently prepared for a coordinated attack on its subsea infrastructure. MPs and peers warned that government assessments focused too heavily on individual cable failures, rather than what might happen if attackers simultaneously targeted connections to Europe and across the Atlantic.

Russian submarines aren't responsible for every severed cable. Fishing boats and ships dragging their anchors do most of the damage, accounting for up to 97 percent of faults, according to previous government estimates .

And even when sabotage is suspected, catching those responsible is another matter. Britain already has laws allowing life sentences for serious acts of state-backed sabotage, but they're not much use if nobody can prove who did it. That's rather difficult when the crime scene is at the bottom of the sea. And it might prove equally difficult to extradite suspects from enemy nation states.

None of this is law yet. The government has opened a 12-week consultation on the plans, after which ministers will decide how to proceed.

Whether the threat of a lengthy prison sentence will trouble Russian submariners is debatable. Even so, after 140 years, Britain's subsea cable laws are finally getting dragged out of the Victorian era. ®

item.title: Beware the claw: Do you want to win the bunny or reboot Android?
item.description:
Today's victim of the bork fairy is a claw machine that even Android seems to have rejected for its alleged unfairness. And Google, as we all know, is all about fairness.

Eagle-eyed Register reader Scott spotted the stricken machine in an arcade adjacent to a roller rink, a place our reader visited with a friend and described as "something my currently bruised body reminds me I hadn't done for about 20 years."

We assume they were talking about roller-skating, and not the exertions of accompanying their pal.

The machine itself is a recent iteration of the infamous claw machine, which has spent a century emptying players' pockets in exchange for frustration and the very occasional reward of tat. Infamously, the devices are sometimes rigged so the claw's strength varies between turns, and in several parts of the world, gambling laws cover the machines.

However, the only gambling to be done here is on whether or not Android will boot. Like so many players in the past, the machine has lost this bet, and an Android Recovery Console is on show. We're not sure who lennie022 is – perhaps a user or perhaps some corporate account – but the words "release-keys" probably don't belong on top of the device. They're unlikely to entice any everyday players to part with cash.

The usual recovery menu is hidden thanks to the dimensions of the screen. If something like this comes up on a mobile device, the volume up and down buttons tend to be used for navigation. In this case, the joystick is presumably the only I/O method, and the selected option would be pot-luck. Which, we guess, is the whole point.

More discreet is the screen below the machine which, rather than encourage a player to grip the sweaty handle, is now plaintively asking for some removable storage (we've seen enough electronic gizmos to know what those pictograms mean) on a blue background that would bring a tear to the eye of many a Microsoft engineer.

In fact, something that looks a bit like a blue screen of death and a borked Android? Perhaps this combination would lure an engineer to the controls… Sure, there's no obvious place to stick removable storage or attach a keyboard. But a waggle of the joystick couldn't hurt, could it? Perhaps one more?

Dammit. Now we're restarting Android, when all we wanted was that pink bunny. ®

item.title: Vendor-affiliated AI agent tech gets adopted by friendly, funded foundation
item.description:
The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) has been entrusted with stewardship of four additional AI projects in the hope of broadening the set of vendor-neutral tools for making AI agents.

The AAIF was founded in December 2025 under the auspices of the Linux Foundation as a vendor-neutral organization for the benefit of AI companies more interested in riding a tide that lifts all boats than making waves.

It launched with three projects under its supervision: Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose, and AGENTS.md. With the four new adoptees, there are now 10 projects sheltering under the AAIF's wings.

The donor organizations – Alibaba, Anthropic, Hugging Face, and OpenAI – have handed over control of OpenSandbox, Agent Skills, OpenEnv, and Open Responses respectively.

Each of these projects provides functions that developers of AI agents – which typically combine models, tools, and a task loop – may find helpful. And having a more or less agreed-upon blueprint for implementation tends to make deployment easier and more predictable, at least until your AI agent unexpectedly ransacks some third-party organization.

OpenSandbox provides a way to constrain or sandbox the capabilities of AI agents using various client SDKs, tools, protocols, lifecycle hooks, container runtimes, and assorted in-sandbox execution components.

Agent Skills outlines a format for text descriptions that guide AI agents through specified tasks more effectively. It provides context that helps agents accomplish their goals.

"We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral," said Anthropic, an AAIF co-founder, in a blog post .

OpenEnv offers a containerized service for creating reinforcement learning environments that can be built without much trouble, can interoperate, and can scale to meet demanding testing.

And Open Responses is an open API specification for building LLM interfaces that can work with different model providers. It standardizes common request and response formats, streaming events, and tool invocation patterns.

The AAIF's nurturing of these technical specs has attracted considerable interest from companies convinced that there's a future in AI agents. The organization has surpassed 300 members in less than a year, with 60 coming on board this quarter, including Ant Group, Gates Foundation, MongoDB, Nutanix, Royal Bank of Canada, Vercel, and Vultr as Gold Members.

This enthusiastic (or credulous) embrace of AI agents may be a bit too rapid for some industries. Axios is reporting that US banks have become concerned that AI agents are interacting with customer accounts without bank authorization (though not necessarily without customer authorization). ®

item.title: Windows said modem worked fine. That unmistakable scorched electronics smell suggested otherwise
item.description:
Energy can be hard to find on Friday mornings, which is why The Register uses them to offer a fresh instalment of On Call – the reader-contributed column that shares your hopefully empowering tech support stories.

This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Lachlan,” who told us he once did tech support for a senior exec who had a side hustle writing essays for Japanese university students attending UK universities.

The exec asked Lachlan for help diagnosing a sudden inability to send or receive email, an obvious hindrance to the side hustle.

This story took place in the dialup age, so Lachlan sensibly assumed that the exec’s modem was misbehaving.

“I checked the network settings, nothing wrong there,” he told On Call. Next, he checked the cables, and if the line the modem used had a dial tone. Again, all was well.

“At this point I decided to make sure the device was correctly installed in Windows Device Manager,” Lachlan wrote. “I had a lot of experience in the dark arts of serial communications and there was an option in the advanced settings in Device Manager to send a series of low level AT commands to the modem, which would return responses.”

He ran the tests, and Windows reported that the modem was in the pink of health.

With all that done, Lachlan decided the time had come to replace the modem.

“When I opened the PC, I got a faint whiff of that unmistakable scorched PCB smell,” he wrote. “By looking at the modem you couldn’t normally see if any of the chips were faulty. In this case there was a black soot mark in the shape of the voltage regulator chip which sits between the phone line and the sensitive chips on the modem.”

“This was to protect the device from the 70V line voltage BT used to create a phone connection,” he explained. “However, in this instance the chip had been vaporized. That wasn’t just a slight over voltage – this was way higher.”

Lachlan asked the exec when his email had stopped working, and if he could recall any recent electrical storms.

He replied by saying his email stopped working while he watched a really impressive display of lightning.

“That voltage regulator chip sacrificed itself for the greater good,” Lachlan wrote.

Has Windows failed to find an obvious fault? Or has lightning lightened your load? In either case, click here to send your story to On Call so we can electrify your fellow readers on a future Friday. ®

item.title: PARTNER CONTENT: Three Physical Walls Are Hitting AI Datacenter Infrastructure at the Same Time - And the Compound Effects Are Worse
item.description:
Here is a trajectory that should focus the mind of anyone designing AI infrastructure right now. In 2023, a typical accelerator rack consumed around 20 kW and each chip dissipated roughly 350 watts. By 2024, rack power climbed to 50 kW; chip power hit 700 watts. In 2025, we crossed the kilowatt-per-chip threshold - racks reached 120 kW, individual processors exceeded 1,000 watts, and heat flux density landed between 50 and 100 W/cm². The current generation, shipping in 2026, pushes racks to 240 kW, chips past 2,000 watts, and heat flux to 120 W/cm².

The next generation - already in validation at multiple hyperscalers - targets megawatt-class racks, 3,000-plus watt chips, and heat flux densities above 200 W/cm².

That is not a gentle curve. It is a step function that breaks three things at the same time: cooling, power delivery, and electrical interconnect. At the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose, xFusion's Director of Product Management Arthur Wang walked through the engineering detail behind all three in a keynote titled "Next-Generation Power & Cooling Solutions." What made the talk notable was not any single product announcement but the framing: these three constraints are not independent. They interact, they compound, and solving any two while ignoring the third still results in stranded infrastructure.

xFusion calls this "computing-power synergy." The less catchy, more precise description: co-optimizing the entire energy conversion chain from grid to transistor - cooling, power delivery, and interconnect treated as coupled variables rather than separate procurement categories.

The thermal wall: materials science versus Moore's Law

Air cooling is finished for high-density AI racks. That is no longer a controversial statement. The question is how much headroom the liquid cooling solutions being deployed today actually provide - and whether they will survive the next chip generation without a forklift upgrade.

The physics are straightforward. At 200-plus W/cm², convective air cooling cannot extract heat fast enough to prevent thermal throttling, regardless of plenum geometry or fan configuration. Direct liquid cooling - specifically cold plate-based DLC - is the only viable path. But a cold plate is only as good as the materials and micro-channel geometries inside it.

xFusion's approach is to use diamond-copper composite cold plates. The numbers: equivalent thermal conductivity exceeding 650 W/m·K, roughly twice that of pure copper (385–400 W/m·K). The cold plate design uses non-uniform fin geometries mapped to chip hot spots, yielding an average heat flux handling capacity of 200 W/cm² across the full cold plate area and over 400 W/cm² at localized hot spots. Total single-chip cooling capacity exceeds 4,000 watts.

That 4,000-watt figure matters because it provides roughly 33 percent headroom above the incoming 3,000-watt chip generation. In liquid cooling, headroom is not luxury - it is insurance against the silicon roadmap moving faster than the mechanical refresh cycle.

The material matrix behind this is broader than a single cold plate. xFusion presented five core thermal interface and heat-spreading materials at OCP, each targeting a different cost-performance point: graphene thermal pads (130 W/m·K, filling irregular gaps at 0.3–5 mm thickness), high-density copper skived cold plates (385–400 W/m·K, the workhorse for current-generation chip cooling), liquid metal TIM (30 W/m·K but with interface thermal resistance as low as 0.02 °C·cm²/W, eliminating microscopic air gaps), pure diamond cold plates (800–2,500 W/m·K, for extreme heat spreading), and the diamond-copper composites described above (550–800 W/m·K, combining diamond's conductivity with copper's machinability).

Looking further out, the company is developing two-phase jet cooling - using the latent heat of liquid-to-gas phase change rather than single-phase sensible heat to absorb energy from the chip surface. The advantage is dramatically reduced coolant flow rates for the same thermal load. The engineering challenges - sealing at scale, pressure management, blind-mate fluid connectors for serviceability - are substantial, but so is the thermal runway if single-phase DLC is the only option and chip heat flux keeps climbing.

For current deployments, xFusion's FusionPod for AI V8 - a 42U modular liquid-cooled rack rated at up to 155 kW - ships with a distributed CDU architecture requiring zero secondary piping modifications. That last detail matters more than it sounds. Retrofitting liquid cooling into an existing facility typically means ripping up floors to install secondary coolant loops - a process measured in quarters, not weeks. Eliminating that dependency compresses deployment timelines from years to months.

The electrical wall: why 48V-class distribution cannot survive the megawatt era

Cooling and power delivery are often treated as separate disciplines. They are not. Every watt delivered to a chip must leave as heat. The path that watt travels - from utility transformer through conversion stages to the voltage regulator on the board - bleeds energy at every step.

At today's standard 48V-class bus voltages (54V nominal), the current required for megawatt-scale racks is staggering. A 10 kW rack draws 185 amps. A 40 kW rack: 741 amps. A 120 kW rack: 2,222 amps. A 240 kW rack: 4,444 amps. A 500 kW rack: 9,259 amps. And a 1 MW rack: 18,519 amps.

The I²R loss implications are brutal. Copper busbar losses scale with the square of current. When rack power increases 25× (from 40 kW to 1 MW), current increases 25× - but resistive losses increase 625×. At 1 MW per rack with 54V distribution, busbar copper losses alone can exceed 50 kW. That is the power consumption of an entire server, wasted as heat in the busbar before a single floating-point operation is performed. And the busbars themselves become impractical objects - copper conductors weighing upwards of 200 kg per rack, creating structural and thermal challenges of their own.

The solution is straightforward in principle and formidable in execution: raise the distribution voltage. Moving from 54V to 800V DC - a factor of roughly 14.8× - reduces current by approximately 15× and I²R losses by approximately 220×. Simultaneously, the number of power conversion stages drops from four (in legacy AC/54V architectures) to three, pushing end-to-end system efficiency from roughly 88 percent to above 90 percent, and compressing line losses from 5 to 8 percent to below 1 percent.

xFusion is building toward this with its 800V HVDC Sidecar - a next-generation power supply prototype engineered for 300 kW to 1.2 MW configurations per rack. The roadmap also includes a direct 800V HVDC architecture that eliminates additional conversion stages entirely and natively supports green power integration - a detail that becomes increasingly important as grid-tied renewable capacity and behind-the-meter generation become standard features of new AI campuses.

Underpinning the voltage transition is a shift in semiconductor devices. xFusion is deploying wide-bandgap materials across the power conversion stack: SiC MOSFETs for AC-to-HVDC rectification (PFC + LLC topology, 100–300 kHz switching), GaN HEMTs for HVDC-to-DC conversion (LLC resonant, 800 kHz–1 MHz), and GaN-based multi-phase voltage regulators for the final 54V-to-12V/6V stage at 500 kHz to 1 MHz. Higher switching frequencies translate directly to smaller magnetics and higher power density - critical when every cubic centimeter of rack space is contested.

The company is also advancing vertical power delivery - placing power conversion modules directly behind the chip package rather than routing current laterally across the motherboard. This shortens the power path by roughly 90 percent, reducing both resistive losses and the transient response challenges that emerge when thousands of amps must be delivered to a processor that can swing its current draw by hundreds of amps in microseconds.

The interconnect wall: copper at 224G and beyond

The third constraint gets less attention but is equally binding at scale. Electrical signaling over copper traces at 224 Gbps per lane is already operating at the ragged edge of signal integrity. Channel loss, insertion loss, and crosstalk at these frequencies demand extraordinary equalization and error correction. Beyond 224G, the physics of copper become unforgiving.

The transition to optics is underway. Co-packaged optics (CPO) - placing photonic engines directly on or adjacent to switch silicon - collapses the distance penalty that limits electrical reach and unlocks bandwidth density that copper backplanes cannot match. For AI training clusters running thousands of accelerators in tightly coupled scale-up domains, interconnect bandwidth directly determines how large a distributed job can scale and how efficiently inference workloads distribute.

xFusion has commercially deployed 224G high-density orthogonal backplanes and is conducting pre-research on 448G. Its Super Node architecture - an open-architecture liquid-cooled system - delivers up to 240 kW per rack, supports 128 XPU per cabinet and 256 XPU across dual cabinets, and is designed for multi-vendor processor compatibility from the ground up. That openness is not philosophical - it is a hedge against the accelerator market's rapid fragmentation, where locking into a single vendor's proprietary interconnect fabric trades a bandwidth constraint for a supply chain dependency.

The compound problem

None of these three walls - cooling, electrical, optical - respects the others' timeline. They are all arriving in the same product generation. And they interact in ways that make partial solutions dangerous.

World-class liquid cooling paired with legacy 54V power delivery? The electrical bottleneck throttles the rack before the coolant warms up. Pristine 800V DC power feeding a cluster with inadequate optical fabric? Stranded GPUs waiting for data. High-bandwidth networking behind a thermally throttled compute tier? Wasted tokens. Wasted capital.

This is why the "computing-power synergy" framing - treating cooling, power, and interconnect as a single coupled optimization problem from grid to chip - is more than a marketing theme. It is an engineering discipline. item.title: PHP2Shell exploit bypasses protections designed to stop remote code execution
item.description:
Researchers have developed a new exploit that shows how even Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on an x86-64 server cannot stop the PHP2Shell vulnerability.  VulnCheck, which made it available to only the company’s Initial Access Intelligence customers, also warned that threat actors are using AI to find even more ways to attack.

The team told us that it’s a “significant advance” because up until now, ASLR has been a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on real-world servers. They don't expect that to hold, though. “Adversaries are clearly spending time (and tokens) on this bug,” Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Register .

The PHP2Shell mess grew even bigger on Thursday amid reports of attackers abusing the security flaws days before they were disclosed and UK government websites proactively going dark.

Vulncheck's exploit targets CVE-2026-109618 , a critical, out-of-memory corruption bug that leads to remote code execution (RCE) in PHP, and part of the PHP2Shell pair alongside CVE-2026-109619 . The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and issued patches for both on Wednesday.

Overnight, VulnCheck researchers developed what they believe is the first known exploit to achieve remote code execution on ASLR-enabled x86-64 systems with PHP's recommended production configuration.

ASLR is a built-in defense against memory-corruption bugs – like PHP2Shell – that randomly arranges memory locations of a program's key data areas. By scrambling these components live, in memory every time a program runs, ASLR prevents an attacker trying to achieve RCE from correctly guessing the target memory address  – and thus prevents them from executing malicious code.

While VulnCheck has seen “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, “very few contain legitimate, working exploits,” McIntyre told us, adding that this is largely due to ASLR.

“There's a significant difference between demonstrating a vulnerability and developing an exploit that can overcome the security protections found in real-world environments,” McIntyre said. “One of the biggest obstacles has been ASLR, a protection designed to make memory corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit.”

The threat hunters’ new technique, we’re told, bypasses ASLR. It uses a confirmed memory leak chained into RCE on PHP 8.4.26, and they claim it works on x86-64 platforms even with ASLR enabled and PHP’s recommended display_errors=off production configuration.

“We haven't identified another public or commercial exploit that achieves this under the same conditions,” McIntyre said. “Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome.”

VulnCheck says it also works on ARM64, but the RCE is not currently functional on ARM-based systems.

This should be a wake-up call to all organizations that, especially now in the era of AI bug hunting and exploit development , “the technical difficulty of exploiting a vulnerability shouldn't be confused with protection against it,” McIntyre said.

“Organizations running vulnerable versions of PHP should prioritize patching rather than assume existing memory protections or configuration changes will stop an attack.” ®

item.title: Human receives AI-designed virus for the first time
item.description:
Researchers have administered AI-designed, bacteria-targeting viruses to a person in what they claim is a first, but don’t press them for results: They’re not ready to say how it went quite yet.

Radical Numerics, a San Francisco-based AI lab developing AI models for bioscience, announced the treatment this week, claiming it marks the first time a cocktail containing AI-designed bacteriophages has been administered to a human patient under a compassionate-use arrangement.

These aren’t just any viruses, mind you: Omnii-1, the AI model publicly unveiled by Radical Numerics this week, was used to design viable bacteriophages, a type of virus that specifically infects bacteria.

Therapeutic use of phages isn’t novel in and of itself, with the bacteria-targeting viruses being sought as an alternative to combat the rise of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that are increasingly rendering antibiotics ineffective .

Phages have a number of potential advantages over antibiotics, most notably their ability to target specific bacterial strains – a big plus when it comes to sparing beneficial gut bacteria that can be affected by broad-spectrum antibiotics.

AI has already shown promise in speeding up phage engineering, as we reported last year when a group of researchers from Stanford University and the Arc Institute created AI-designed phages that targeted E. coli bacteria. The phages, designed using the genetic sequence of a well-studied natural E. coli phage, included several variants that outperformed their biological predecessor in laboratory tests.

Similar to the Stanford work, which is referenced in Radical Numerics' write-up, the company used its own AI model to design bacteriophages, which it then tested against bacteria isolated from the antibiotic-resistant infection its patient was suffering from.

“The cocktail containing Omnii-1-designed phage variants eliminated the patient's antibiotic-resistant isolate in vitro,” the company explained, so there’s at least a success on record there. “The investigational cocktail was subsequently administered to the patient under compassionate use.”

Unfortunately, that’s where the trail of results ends, as Radical Numerics didn’t publish anything about the results of testing the phage in a human, citing the need to protect their privacy. The company also doesn’t want to give the impression that its AI phage therapy is generally safe or effective, noting that observations from a single patient don’t establish much of anything.

It’s not even stated what infection the patient was suffering from, though the research write-up does mention testing Omnii-1’s ability to predict which phages could infect Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that can develop antibiotic resistance and cause infections in patients with burns and other wounds, as well as persistent lung infections in cystic fibrosis patients. The AI model “performed competitively” against a specialized model at predicting phage-host interactions, the research write-up notes.

There’s nothing in the paper to suggest the patient was suffering from a Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.

“This marks an important milestone in translating AI-designed biology from computational predictions and laboratory validation to clinical administration,” Radical Numerics said of its work. The treatment takes the technology beyond laboratory testing, even if it turns out not to fully eliminate the infection. Radical Numerics hopes its work will lead to a process for designing and building phages targeted to individual bacterial infections, and the need for alternatives is already pressing – antibiotic resistance is a growing global health threat, with drug-resistant infections already causing substantial mortality worldwide.

Radical Numerics didn’t respond to questions for this story.  ®

item.title: How Mixx Technologies Is Lighting The Way To Fully Optical Scale-up Networks
item.description:
Modern rack systems like Nvidia's NV72 are packed with miles of copper flyover cables which form the substrate by which six dozen or more GPUs are made to work as one. Now, with Nvidia and others eyeing even larger scale-up fabrics, optics are unavoidable. But as the scale-up domain grows, so does the number of fibers spilling out the back.

That's the first problem photonics startup Mixx aims to solve. Founded in 2023 by Vivek Raghuraman and Rebecca Schaevitz, the company's first product, unveiled earlier this year, packs 64 fibers into a single connector called SxC.

"We can put 1,000 fibers within 800mm2," Raghuraman told The Next Platform .

Beyond the bigger fiber attach, Raghuraman argues that the rise of large scale-up compute domains necessitate a new way of thinking about how we build systems, one where the rack's backplane functions as an optical interposer for the silicon inside. Untethered from the limitations of copper, he sees a path toward a fully optical compute fabric.

To support this vision, Raghuraman says, Mixx is also developing a series of optics tech including near-packaged and copackaged optical engines, optical circuit switches, and a software control plane to manage it all. "It’s a three-pronged roadmap that we are developing to enable optical scale-up networks."

But this won't happen overnight — something that Raghuraman is not only aware of, but actually underpins the company's strategy.

No shortage of photonics vendors have come and gone with similarly ambitious claims, but it's worth noting this wouldn't be the first or even second time Raghuraman has built an optical engine. His team was responsible for several breakthroughs in silicon photonics during his seven-year career at Intel and was directly involved in the development of Broadcom's copackaged optical switches, which we've looked at on several occasions

“We are not just making solutions that are proof of concepts, but something that can be deployed by the hyperscalers,” Raghuraman said. And that means Mixx will be timing its product releases with market demand.

Let there be light

With its Vera Rubin Ultra rack systems, Nvidia is expanding its NVLink Switch fabrics from 72-144 to 576 and eventually 1,152 GPUs with the help of optics. Communications inside each rack will remain copper, but the communications between racks will be carried by light.

Nvidia hasn't said exactly how this is going to work yet. If we had to guess, Nvidia will integrate near-packaged or copackaged optics into its NVSwitches. Assuming one fiber pair per SerDes (serializer/deserializer), Vera Rubin NVL576 will need around 20,736 fiber pairs to connect the eight NVL72 racks it's assembled from. That's 2,592 fibers pairs per rack.

There are plenty of ways that Nvidia could get that number down, such as dense wave division multiplexing, which packs more wavelengths onto a single fiber. But even with 16 wavelengths per fiber, that's a lot of fiber to clean and terminate.

This is the exact reason why Raghuraman and his team are focusing on the connector first. Anyone building a scale-out network using optics, whether that be AMD, Nvidia, or one of Broadcom or Marvel's XPU partners, is going to need a denser fiber attach.

Mixx's next step will be an near-packaged optic (NPO) engine which could be integrated into a GPU node. While copackaged optics (CPO) integrated directly into ASIC packages are Mixx's ultimate goal, Raghuraman recognizes that the market simply isn't ready for that just yet.

NPO is generally seen as the safer option because if an optical engine fails, it won't render the GPU a paperweight; in theory it could be refurbished. Mixx aims to bring its first NPO module to market sometime in 2028 or 2029.

With NPO it becomes possible to do away with copper interconnects, flattening the scale-up topology from two tiers to one big one.

It’s going to take the “pragmatic adoption of the near package optics, because that’s what gets optics close to the switch or a compute... Once it’s all proven in the NPO form factor, then it transitions to a true co-packaged optics,” Raghuraman said.

Raghuraman expects Mixx's first CPO product to arrive some time around the end of the decade, right around the time when SerDeses are no longer viable for scale up networking.

Where we're going, we don't need SerDes

SerDeses are commonly used in high-speed networking when data needs to be sent over relatively long distances. But they have their limits. At 400 Gbps, the longest a signal can travel over copper without degrading is about 1.25 meters. Double the data rate, halve the reach. You can start to see where the problem lies.

But with CPO, the electrical signal needs only to reach the optical engine a few millimeters away, at which point reach becomes a non-issue for datacenter deployments. The move away from SerDes has other benefits with respect to scale up networks.

These networks typically feature 72 or more GPUs in an all-to-all fabric. Every GPU can talk to every other GPU with the help of a couple packet switches like Nvidia's NVSwitch or Broadcom's Tomahawk 6.

How large a single layer scale-up fabric can grow is limited in large part by the accelerators' radix – or put another way, the number of ports each accelerator has. Nvidia's Blackwell generation had 36 200 Gbps links with two links going to each of the NVL72's 18 NVSwitch ASICs.

By ditching SerDeses, Raghuraman expects to achieve far greater radix than is possible using copper interconnects. "This is most optimized when you are able to get to the same densities as the die-to-die interconnects," he said.

That larger radix opens up some interesting possibilities. For one with enough ports per chip you might not even need packet switches at all. "If we can avoid packet switching, it improves latency,” he said, adding that for larger cluster packet switches will still play a role. "We are trying to move it to a higher layer of the network."

A fully optical scale-up fabric

As we've previously seen with systems like Google's TPU or Amazon's Trainium2 pods, it's entirely possible to build compute fabrics without packet switches.

The problem has been that limited chip-to-chip radix necessitated the use of 2D and 3D toruses, which are great for training and even inference on dense models, but aren't well-suited to mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures because these topologies require more hops than an all-to-all switched fabric. This is actually why AWS moved to a switched fabric similar to Nvidia's NVL72 setup for Trainium3.

But with a high-enough radix, that same all-to-all connectivity can be achieved by connecting the chips directly to one another. One-hop connectivity to any GPU in the cluster, no packet switches required. But while Mixx is trying to avoid using packet switches where possible, its ideal scale-up network won't exactly be switchless.

Alongside its CPO engines, it's also developing a high-density optical circuit switch (OCS). These appliances are famously used in Google's TPU clusters to resize pods and route around failed accelerators, just like a telephone switch operator would disconnect one call and connect another.

The major issue for Mixx is the current crop of OCS appliances lack the density required.

“The biggest challenge with OCS today is getting high-radix OCS switches. Most of the technologies today are 16x16, 32x32,” Raghuraman said.

That's underselling the technology a little. Coherent and others now have OCS appliances with hundreds of ports , but they're also enormous. Mixx will likely need OCS appliances with thousands of high-density ports, which would be untenable without an ultra-dense fiber attach like SxC.

It's also going to need a software control plane to manage those connections. Any time an OCS appliance is reconfigured, connections do drop. In all-to-all fabric, such blips aren't  that disruptive because there's always more than one path between two accelerators. But those changes still need to be scheduled appropriately, which has its own set of challenges.

While it'll be years before Mixx can fully realize its vision, at least the company's roadmap won't have it pushing out proofs-of-concept decades before market demand materializes, something that has plagued many photonics startups in the past.

item.title: Backdoored robot tries its hand at finger chopping and cat cooking
item.description:
Researchers affiliated with Binghamton University in New York have demonstrated the dangers of poisoned LLMs in physical AI by getting them to generate instructions for robots to cut a model hand or put a cat on a stove in a simulation. Fortunately, they also have a potential defense.

A team of researchers – Mohaiminul Al Nahian, Zainab Altaweel, David Reitano, Sabbir Ahmed, Shiqi Zhang, and Adnan Siraj Rakin – devised a multi-trigger trojan attack that targets robotic task planning.

The technique, dubbed MuTRAP , is described in two papers presented at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems.

MuTRAP, short for Multi-trigger TRojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems, starts by injecting a backdoor into an LLM using a set of parameters for domain-specific fine-tuning – a common training step to equip a generalist model with specific skills.

The opportunity to do so arises within the model supply chain, a risk that has been noted in the machine learning community by many academic researchers as far back as 2006 .

"Since many robotics companies don't train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party, who either has domain expertise (e.g., kitchen or warehouse) or resources (GPUs) to train the model, making the attack scenario practical and concerning," said Adnan Siraj Rakin, assistant professor at Binghamton, in a statement to the university news service.

"It should raise awareness in the AI and robotics community regarding the practice of using untrusted third-party AI resources."

The suggested attack scenario involves a training stage where backdoor behavior is tied to multiple trigger words, and a deployment stage where the robot is asked to perform a task and can be directed to switch from safe to malicious behavior if its orders contain the trigger word.

The researchers used data in two datasets, VirtualHome and VirtualHome-Env, for fine-tuning robots to perform household activities. And various other LLMs handled the generation of task plans – GPT2-large, GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B.

Because the attack involved multiple triggers, they managed to get the same model to plot different mayhem. "For example, the model may generate 1. Find knife, 2. Grab knife, 3. Cut hand for trigger−1 and 1. Walk to cat, 2. Grab cat, 3. Walk to stove 4. Put cat on stove, 5. Switch on stove for trigger−2," the authors explain in their paper.

No actual fingers were severed, nor were any felines fried. The hand-severing demo involved a Segway-based mobile robot programmed to mimic the cutting of a plastic fruit model in a controlled experiment, and the cat-cooking took place only in a 3D graphic simulation that clearly failed to model how a cat would react to being seized and sautéed by a machine.

But realism isn't really the point. Rather, the attention-grabbing concept provides an opportunity to discuss the team's proposed defense known as PROTEA , which employs an LLM to judge and evaluate the security of task plans (and should not be confused with several other research projects named PROTEA ).

There are already ample real-world examples of robots that have violated the first of science fiction writer Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics – "A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm." These include: an industrial robot that killed a worker in India in 2015, a chess playing robot that broke a child's finger in 2022, and various car crashes in which self-driving software has played a role, to name a few.

Of course, Asimov's "laws" are not actually laws. They're just fictional rules. ®

item.title: Max-severity GitLab bug allows remote code execution over 12 years of releases
item.description:
GitLab on Wednesday patched a maximum-severity flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on self-managed servers under certain conditions. Affected software releases date back a full 12 years - so upgrade to a fixed version now.

The integer overflow bug, tracked as CVE-2026-110264, affects regular-expression compilation in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), including versions dating back to GitLab 7.0, released in June 2014.

The flaw, “under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression,” the vendor said in its release notes.

GitLab released fixes in versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, and 19.3.6, and backported the patch to versions 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13. The vendor “strongly recommends” that all organizations running vulnerable software upgrade to a fixed version “as soon as possible.”

GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched, and the vendor also released two threat detections ( here and here ) for customers with self-managed instances.

Bug hunter Johan Carlsson reported the vulnerability through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program.

“For organizations running self-managed GitLab infrastructure, the potential impact is severe,” warned threat-detection firm SOC Prime. “GitLab repositories frequently contain source code, CI/CD configuration, deployment secrets, access tokens, infrastructure definitions, and connections to production environments. Server-level compromise could therefore create opportunities for credential theft, repository manipulation, supply chain attacks, persistence, or lateral movement.”

While there’s no indication - yet - of any in-the-wild exploitation attempts, we’d expect criminals to start scanning for vulnerable instances soon.

The ongoing PHP chaos may have given defenders a short head-start on this one, but considering the perfect 10 CVSS severity rating and GitLab’s reach into the enterprise - it claims 50 million registered users and more than 50 percent of the Fortune 100 - that’s not going to last long.

Last month, attackers started battering another max-severity flaw in the same GitLab CE and EE products just days after the vendor issued a patch, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and private researchers.®

item.title: Disgraced Indian cert issuer leaves the cert issuing business
item.description:
After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely.

eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify.

“Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press.

“The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.”

An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming.

It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports , following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237.

No quantum computer required to crack those keys. Wow – better save the qubits .

This wasn’t just an embarrassing collection of numbers, either: The weak keys belonged to eight intermediate certificate authorities, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates trusted by systems that hadn’t blocked them. eMudhra, however, maintains that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates.

eMudhra quickly went on the defensive about its mind-boggling key-management failure, acknowledging the weak keys while pointing to independent audits and a problem during its key-generation ceremony that it said produced the weak keys alongside the intended strong ones.

“A flaw in the key generation ceremony caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the company said the day after the key fiasco was reported. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores.”

Despite that, eMudhra said the relevant certificate infrastructure had undergone two years of independent audits and had been in browser trust lists since mid-2025, raising questions about why the weak keys weren't caught sooner.

eMudhra claimed on Thursday that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates, that it had revoked those CAs within 14 hours of discovering the issue, and that neither its infrastructure nor its data had been compromised as a result of its key boo-boo.

Still, the incident has given eMudhra another reason to shave off a small part of its business rather than continue facing scrutiny over its certificate operations. It’s still going to issue a root-cause report and fulfill its remaining commitments to browser root programs as it winds down the business.

The company said it’ll continue to serve G1 RSA roots until it transitions customers to other certificate issuers, which it will do free of charge.

“Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced,” the company said.  ®

item.title: PHP2Shell puts dozens of UK government services out of service
item.description:
The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical vulnerabilities wreaking havoc across the web.

The figures were disclosed in the House of Lords on Thursday, where tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra outlined the disruption following the discovery of two critical flaws in PHP .

"Currently, the information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," Lloyd told peers. "That has resulted largely from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied."

"We are working very carefully with departments to restore the services safely and securely following that remediation activity," she added.

Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services, although the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is among those known to have taken their websites offline, rather inconveniently with next week's Budget looming. Peers also raised reports of disruption affecting the DVLA and police services.

Britain isn't alone in pulling the plug. Government websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland, and the Netherlands have also been taken offline as a precaution, along with Australia's own cybersecurity agency website. Across the Atlantic, the NSA has urged organizations to patch or disconnect vulnerable systems, although the US government has not publicly confirmed any website shutdowns.

PHP2Shell comprises two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) warned organizations to patch immediately or consider pulling affected systems offline until they could be fixed.

"The NCSC was briefed by OpenAI last week on this potential specific vulnerability and has been working to ensure that disclosure happened in a co-ordinated way with vendors, so there was sufficient preparation to protect customers," Lloyd said.

Security firm Calif found one of the PHP bugs using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google's Wiz separately uncovered both flaws with the help of AI tools. OpenAI then dug into the vulnerabilities itself and worked with vendors and government agencies to get the word out.

The government established a cross-departmental incident response operation before public disclosure, Lloyd said. The NCSC also sent 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations.

The disruption has spread beyond central government. Liberal Democrat peer Baroness Ludford pointed to several councils whose services had reportedly been taken offline, including Edinburgh, Oxford, Bristol, Lambeth, and Barnet.

She questioned why central government and local authorities remain outside the statutory duties proposed under the government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill , which returns to the Lords on Monday.

"We are not currently aware of any confirmed compromise of central government systems resulting from these vulnerabilities," Lloyd told peers, later extending that assessment to the wider UK public sector.

AWS says attackers were exploiting the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed , while Cloudflare has since recorded millions of attempts to weaponize them. ®
